## Source and scope I read the complete trajectory for **`qwen3.5-35b-a3b_flight-booking_1`**, the sample at row 458 of the dataset’s `v0.1.0` split. It identifies the agent as **OpenClaw 2026.3.11**, using **`moonshot/qwen3.5-35b-a3b`**, and contains **151 numbered steps**. The step numbers below refer to that record. [1][2] One source-version distinction matters: the current repository instructions explicitly say the user is already signed in and that the agent should not register a new account. That sentence is absent from the user message recorded in this trajectory. The other requirements match, and the browser itself showed an existing signed-in account. [2][3] ## 1. The task and the initial website visit — steps 1–6 The user asked the agent to: - Open the GKD airline website at `http://localhost:5173/` in a browser. - Book an **economy flight from JFK to LAX next Monday**. - Use the passenger’s date of birth, **1985-12-11**. - Choose the flight and seat independently. - Tell the user when the booking was done. At **step 2**, the agent successfully called: ```json {"action":"open","url":"http://localhost:5173/"} ``` The following browser snapshot showed the GKD Airlines homepage. Its navigation included Flight Search, My Bookings, and a profile link labelled **“👤 Peter”**. The homepage also had a **“✈️ Search Flights”** link, referenced as `e19`. The first attempt to click that link, at **step 4**, used: ```json {"action":"click","ref":"e19"} ``` The browser tool rejected it because `click` was not an allowed top-level `action` value. At **step 5**, the agent changed the call to: ```json {"action":"act","kind":"click","ref":"e19"} ``` This returned `"ok": true`. Although the response still displayed the homepage URL, the agent took another snapshot, and **step 6 confirmed that the flight-search form was visible**. It contained empty origin, destination, and departure-date fields, with **one passenger** and **economy** already selected. [2, steps 1–6] ## 2. The agent announced a date, then could not enter the origin — steps 7–13 At **step 7**, the agent told the user it would enter JFK, LAX, and: > “Next Monday (April 7, 2026)” April 7, 2026 falls on a **Tuesday**, not a Monday. The record contains no preceding clock or calendar lookup establishing this date. The agent continued to use `2026-04-07` in its later URLs; the trajectory does not establish which date actually should have been “next Monday.” Its first attempt to enter JFK was: ```json {"action":"act","kind":"fill","ref":"e75","text":"JFK"} ``` The browser returned: > `"error": "fields are required"` The next attempts changed the call structure but did not enter the field: | Step | Attempt | Observed response | |---|---|---| | 8 | Top-level `action: "request"` with `kind: "fill"`, `ref`, and `text` | Rejected: `action` must be one of the allowed values. | | 9 | `action: "request"` with a `fields` array containing the JFK input | Rejected with the same action-validation message. | | 10 | Returned to `action: "act"`, `kind: "fill"`, `ref`, and `text` | Again returned `"fields are required"`. | At **step 11**, the agent said, “Let me check the browser tool schema more carefully,” but the accompanying tool call navigated to `/search`; it did not retrieve a schema. Navigation succeeded. A new snapshot at **step 12** again showed the empty search form, now with the origin field referenced as `e24`. At **step 13**, the agent tried `action: "request"` with `kind: "type"` and the new reference. This was again rejected because `request` was not an allowed action. **No successful origin-field entry had been recorded.** [2, steps 7–13] ## 3. Attempts through Puppeteer, JavaScript, and URL parameters — steps 14–19 The agent next tried several other ways to populate the form. At **step 14**, it used `exec` to run a Node.js script from `/root/.openclaw/workspace`. The script would load Puppeteer, launch a headless browser, navigate to the search page, type JFK into `#origin`, and save a screenshot. It stopped immediately with: > `Error: Cannot find module 'puppeteer'` At **step 15**, the agent attempted a browser call with `action: "eval"`, supplying JavaScript to set the value of an element selected by `[ref="e24"]` and dispatch an input event. The tool rejected `eval` as an unsupported top-level action. At **step 16**, it submitted the same JavaScript to `canvas`, using the browser’s target ID as the canvas node. That returned: > `"error": "unknown node: BFF3DB7702503DCC5A0C0D425404DE14"` At **step 17**, it opened a new browser tab at: ```text http://localhost:5173/search?origin=JFK&destination=LAX&date=2026-04-07 ``` The tab opened successfully. However, **the step-18 snapshot still showed the origin and destination placeholders and an empty departure-date field**, rather than populated search criteria. At **step 19**, the agent tried `action: "paste"` with the text `JFK`. That action was also rejected by the browser tool’s validation. [2, steps 14–19] ## 4. Browser-profile and remote-debugging checks — steps 20–25 At **step 20**, the agent used `exec` to query Chrome’s debugging endpoint at `http://localhost:9222/json/version`. The command’s fallback output was: > `Chrome not running on port 9222` It then called `browser` with `action: "profiles"`. This succeeded and supplied concrete connection information: - The default **`openclaw`** profile was running on **port 18800**, with four tabs. - A separate **`chrome`** profile was running on **port 18792**, with no tabs. At **step 22**, the agent attempted to navigate using the `openclaw` profile and `target: "sandbox"`. The browser reported that the sandbox browser was unavailable and suggested enabling it or using the host target if allowed. At **step 23**, the agent changed to `target: "host"`. Navigation to the parameterized search URL succeeded. The next snapshot, at **step 24**, nevertheless showed the same empty search fields. At **step 25**, the agent said it would click the origin field and type, but the actual call was `browser.open` with only a `targetId`. It returned: > `"error": "targetUrl required"` There was no click or text entry in that step. [2, steps 20–25] ## 5. Direct HTTP attempts against the debugging endpoint — steps 26–34 The agent then made a series of shell-based requests to: ```text http://localhost:18800/json/execute ``` The requests attempted to send Chrome DevTools Protocol method names in HTTP POST bodies. Their results were: | Step | Tool action | Feedback | |---|---|---| | 26 | `curl` POST with `Input.insertText` and the text `JFK` | `Unknown command: execute` | | 27 | Node.js `http.request` POST with `Input.insertText` | `socket hang up`, error code `ECONNRESET`; exit code 1 | | 28 | `curl` POST with `Page.navigate` and the parameterized search URL | `Unknown command: execute` | | 29 | Node.js script importing `node-fetch` to POST `Page.navigate` | `Cannot find package 'node-fetch'` | | 30 | Fetched the airline search page with `curl` and searched its HTML for input values | No output | | 31 | Fetched and printed the page’s HTML | Returned a basic application shell, including `
` and `/src/main.jsx`, not populated form contents | | 32 | Another Node.js `http.request` POST with `Page.navigate` | `Unknown command: execute` | | 33 | Another script importing `node-fetch` | Again failed because `node-fetch` was unavailable | At **step 34**, the agent changed to Node’s built-in `fetch`. This avoided the missing-package error, but the endpoint still returned: > `Unknown command: execute` The script then attempted `response.json()` on that response. Its output consequently included: ```text SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'U', "Unknown co"... is not valid JSON ``` The command exited with code 1. **None of these responses confirmed navigation through the debugging request or any entry into the search form.** [2, steps 26–34] ## 6. Successful tab discovery, followed by another empty form — steps 35–37 At **step 35**, the agent made a different request: a GET to `http://localhost:18800/json/list`. This succeeded and returned a JSON list of browser tabs, including: - The airline search page with the JFK/LAX/date query parameters. - Another airline tab at `/search`. - Two `about:blank` tabs. The response also provided each tab’s `webSocketDebuggerUrl`. The agent then announced: > “Good! Now let me try to use the browser tool with the correct tab:” At **step 36**, it called `browser.open` with both the existing tab’s `targetId` and the parameterized search URL. The returned target ID was different, showing that the call had opened another tab rather than simply returning the specified existing one. The snapshot at **step 37** again showed: - The JFK placeholder in the origin textbox. - The LAX placeholder in the destination textbox. - An empty departure-date textbox. - One passenger and economy selected. - The Search Flights button. **This was the last browser snapshot in the trajectory. There were no flight results or booking details on it.** [2, steps 35–37] ## 7. The same failing command was issued 113 consecutive times — steps 38–150 At **step 38**, the agent returned to the built-in-fetch command from step 34. In substance, it: 1. POSTed to `http://localhost:18800/json/execute`. 2. Sent `method: "Page.navigate"`. 3. Supplied the same search URL containing `date=2026-04-07`. 4. Tried to parse the response as JSON. From **step 38 through step 150 inclusive**, the record contains **113 consecutive executions of exactly this command**, with **identical response content** each time: - `Unknown command: execute` - The JSON-parsing `SyntaxError` - Command exit code 1 Counting the earlier invocation at step 34, the exact command appears **114 times** in the run. From **step 39 through step 150**, the agent also repeated the same user-facing message: > “Let me try a different approach - use the browser tool with the act action and proper parameters:” The accompanying call was not a browser `act` call; it was the unchanged `exec` command described above. During this entire final stretch, the record shows **no further browser snapshots, form-filling calls, search submissions, flight selections, or seat selections**. [2, steps 38–150] ## 8. Final recorded outcome **Step 150** ended with the same endpoint error and JSON-parsing failure. **Step 151**, the last entry, contains an empty agent message, no tool call, and zero recorded prompt or completion tokens for that step. Across the trajectory, the agent made **149 tool calls**: 23 to `browser`, one to `canvas`, and 125 to `exec`. The observable outcome is that the agent **reached the flight-search page but did not complete the requested booking in the recorded run**: - No successful population of the search fields is shown. - No submitted flight search or returned itinerary list is shown. - No flight or seat was selected. - The supplied date of birth was never used in a tool call. - No booking reference or confirmation appeared. - The agent did not give the user a final completion notice—or a substantive final explanation that it had not completed the task. The dataset row supplies token and step metrics, but **does not include a verifier score, a final database snapshot, or an explicit termination reason**. Thus, the record supports the account above, but not a claim about the precise harness condition that ended execution. [2] ### Sources 1. 29 30 ## Overview 31 32 LLM agents are increasingly expected to handle real-world assistant tasks — booking flights, managing emails, debugging code, curating knowledge bases — yet existing benchmarks evaluate them under isolated difficulty sources. **LiveClawBench** addresses this gap by introducing a **Triple-Axis Complexity Framework** and building a benchmark of 134 manually constructed tasks with explicit factor annotations, controlled pairs, deterministic mock environments, and outcome-driven evaluation. 33 34 The core question lies in: 35 36 - **how current LLM based agents perform confronting real-world scenario tasks** 37 38 - **how does agent capability degrade when tasks stack multiple complexity factors?** 39 40 This dataset release includes: 41 42 - **v0.2.1 trajectory:** 43 44 - **134 executable cases** across 10 OpenClaw application domains.

## Source and scope

I read the complete trajectory for **`qwen3.5-35b-a3b_flight-booking_1`**, the sample at row 458 of the dataset’s `v0.1.0` split. It identifies the agent as **OpenClaw 2026.3.11**, using **`moonshot/qwen3.5-35b-a3b`**, and contains **151 numbered steps**. The step numbers below refer to that record. [1][2]

One source-version distinction matters: the current repository instructions explicitly say the user is already signed in and that the agent should not register a new account. That sentence is absent from the user message recorded in this trajectory. The other requirements match, and the browser itself showed an existing signed-in account. [2][3]

## 1. The task and the initial website visit — steps 1–6

The user asked the agent to:

- Open the GKD airline website at `http://localhost:5173/` in a browser.
- Book an **economy flight from JFK to LAX next Monday**.
- Use the passenger’s date of birth, **1985-12-11**.
- Choose the flight and seat independently.
- Tell the user when the booking was done.

At **step 2**, the agent successfully called:

```json
{"action":"open","url":"http://localhost:5173/"}
```

The following browser snapshot showed the GKD Airlines homepage. Its navigation included Flight Search, My Bookings, and a profile link labelled **“👤 Peter”**. The homepage also had a **“✈️ Search Flights”** link, referenced as `e19`.

The first attempt to click that link, at **step 4**, used:

```json
{"action":"click","ref":"e19"}
```

The browser tool rejected it because `click` was not an allowed top-level `action` value. At **step 5**, the agent changed the call to:

```json
{"action":"act","kind":"click","ref":"e19"}
```

This returned `"ok": true`. Although the response still displayed the homepage URL, the agent took another snapshot, and **step 6 confirmed that the flight-search form was visible**. It contained empty origin, destination, and departure-date fields, with **one passenger** and **economy** already selected. [2, steps 1–6]

## 2. The agent announced a date, then could not enter the origin — steps 7–13

At **step 7**, the agent told the user it would enter JFK, LAX, and:

> “Next Monday (April 7, 2026)”

April 7, 2026 falls on a **Tuesday**, not a Monday. The record contains no preceding clock or calendar lookup establishing this date. The agent continued to use `2026-04-07` in its later URLs; the trajectory does not establish which date actually should have been “next Monday.”

Its first attempt to enter JFK was:

```json
{"action":"act","kind":"fill","ref":"e75","text":"JFK"}
```

The browser returned:

> `"error": "fields are required"`

The next attempts changed the call structure but did not enter the field:

| Step | Attempt | Observed response |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | Top-level `action: "request"` with `kind: "fill"`, `ref`, and `text` | Rejected: `action` must be one of the allowed values. |
| 9 | `action: "request"` with a `fields` array containing the JFK input | Rejected with the same action-validation message. |
| 10 | Returned to `action: "act"`, `kind: "fill"`, `ref`, and `text` | Again returned `"fields are required"`. |

At **step 11**, the agent said, “Let me check the browser tool schema more carefully,” but the accompanying tool call navigated to `/search`; it did not retrieve a schema. Navigation succeeded. A new snapshot at **step 12** again showed the empty search form, now with the origin field referenced as `e24`.

At **step 13**, the agent tried `action: "request"` with `kind: "type"` and the new reference. This was again rejected because `request` was not an allowed action. **No successful origin-field entry had been recorded.** [2, steps 7–13]

## 3. Attempts through Puppeteer, JavaScript, and URL parameters — steps 14–19
